[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"PostgreSQL Streaming Replication: Synchronous vs Asynchronous"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"PostgreSQL streaming replication is a core mechanism for achieving high availability, read scaling, and disaster recovery. It allows a standby server to stay synchronized with a primary server by streaming Write-Ahead Log (WAL) records in real time. Understanding the differences between asynchronous and synchronous replication is vital for balancing data safety (Durability) and write performance (Latency)."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"How PostgreSQL Streaming Replication Works"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"At a high level, the primary server generates WAL records for every transaction. In streaming replication, a background WAL sender process on the primary transmits these records over a network socket to a WAL receiver process on the standby. The standby applies these records to its local storage, ensuring its state mirrors the primary."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Asynchronous Replication"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"In asynchronous mode, the primary server commits transactions and returns a success status to the client as soon as the local WAL is written to disk. It does not wait for the standby server to receive or apply the WAL records."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Pros: High performance, zero network latency penalty for client transactions, and the primary remains operational even if the standby goes offline."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cons: Risk of data loss (RPO > 0) in the event of a sudden primary crash, as recently committed transactions may not have reached the standby yet."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Synchronous Replication"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"In synchronous mode, the primary server waits to return a commit success to the client until the standby server has confirmed that the corresponding WAL records have been written to its local disk. This guarantees zero data loss upon failover."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Pros: Strong consistency, zero data loss (RPO = 0), making it ideal for financial or strict enterprise applications."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cons: Increased transaction latency due to network round-trips, and potential application stalls if the standby server becomes unresponsive or network connectivity drops."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Configuration Guide"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"To configure replication, you must adjust settings in the postgresql.conf file on the primary server. Below is an example of setting up asynchronous streaming replication."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"# postgresql.conf on Primary (Asynchronous)
wal_level = replica
max_wal_senders = 10
wal_keep_size = 1GB"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"To switch from asynchronous to synchronous replication, you must define the synchronous_commit parameter and specify which standby servers are required to acknowledge commits using synchronous_standby_names."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"# postgresql.conf on Primary (Synchronous)
synchronous_commit = on
synchronous_standby_names = 'FIRST 1 (standby_node_1, standby_node_2)'"},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Monitoring Replication Status"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can monitor the real-time status of your streaming replicas by querying the pg_stat_replication system view on the primary server."},{"order":20,"type":"code","text":"SELECT application_name, client_addr, state, sync_state, sync_priority FROM pg_stat_replication;"},{"order":21,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Choosing between synchronous and synchronous PostgreSQL replication depends entirely on your business requirements. Use asynchronous replication when read scalability and low latency are paramount, and use synchronous replication when zero data loss is a strict operational mandate."}]
